| `writing-plans` | 152 | Convert approved spec into a plan of bite-sized (2–5 min) TDD steps with exact paths, full code, no placeholders. |
| `executing-plans` | 70 | Inline (no-subagent) plan execution: load plan, review critically, execute tasks, stop on blockers. Explicitly second-choice to subagent-driven. |
| `subagent-driven-development` | 279 | Execute a plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task + two-stage review (spec compliance, then code quality) per task. |
| `dispatching-parallel-agents` | 182 | One agent per independent problem domain, dispatched concurrently (e.g. 3 unrelated failing test files). |
| `test-driven-development` | 371 | Strict red-green-refactor; Iron Law: "NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST" — code written before test must be deleted. |
| `systematic-debugging` | 296 | Four phases (root cause → pattern analysis → hypothesis → implementation); 3+ failed fixes = question the architecture. |
| `using-git-worktrees` | 215 | Ensure isolated workspace: detect existing isolation → prefer native tools (EnterWorktree) → fall back to `git worktree add` under `.worktrees/`. |
| `finishing-a-development-branch` | 251 | End-of-work ritual: verify tests → detect environment → present exactly 4 options (merge local / push+PR / keep / discard) → cleanup. |
| `requesting-code-review` | 103 | Dispatch a code-reviewer subagent with git SHA range + template; mandatory after each task and before merge. |
| `receiving-code-review` | 213 | Verify-before-implement feedback handling; forbids performative agreement ("You're absolutely right!"); skeptical of external reviewers. |
| `verification-before-completion` | 139 | Iron Law: "NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE" — run the command in this message or don't claim it. |
| `using-superpowers` | 117 | Meta-skill injected at SessionStart; "even 1% chance a skill applies → MUST invoke"; rationalization table; process skills before implementation skills. |
| `writing-skills` | 655 | How to author/test skills: TDD-for-docs, CSO (Claude Search Optimization), token budgets (<150 lines/section), bulletproofing against rationalization, pressure-testing with subagents. |

**Supporting files (not SKILL.md):**
- `subagent-driven-development/`: `implementer-prompt.md`, `spec-reviewer-prompt.md`, `code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md`
- `requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md` (4.7K reviewer prompt template)
- `systematic-debugging/`: `root-cause-tracing.md`, `defense-in-depth.md`, `condition-based-waiting.md` (+example.ts), `find-polluter.sh`, pressure-test fixtures (`test-pressure-1..3.md`)
- `test-driven-development/testing-anti-patterns.md` (8.1K)
- `writing-skills/`: `anthropic-best-practices.md` (44.7K), `graphviz-conventions.dot`, `persuasion-principles.md`, `testing-skills-with-subagents.md` (12.3K)
- `brainstorming/visual-companion.md` (browser-based mockup companion)
- Hooks: `hooks/hooks.json` (SessionStart on startup|clear|compact) + `hooks/session-start` (bash script that injects the full text of `using-superpowers` SKILL.md as additionalContext — multi-platform: Claude Code/Cursor/Copilot detection)
- Multi-harness packaging: `.claude-plugin/`, `.codex-plugin/`, `.cursor-plugin/`, `.opencode/`, `GEMINI.md`

## 2. Lifecycle coverage and chaining

**Covered stages:** idea → design/spec → plan → execute → per-task review → finish (merge/PR). Plus orthogonal disciplines: TDD, debugging, verification, review reception.

**The canonical chain (each skill explicitly names the next as "REQUIRED SUB-SKILL"):**

```
brainstorming
  → writes spec to docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md
  → user-approval gate → invokes writing-plans (the ONLY allowed next skill)
writing-plans
  → writes plan to docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature>.md
  → plan header itself embeds: "REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: use subagent-driven-development
    (recommended) or executing-plans"
  → offers user choice: Subagent-Driven vs Inline
subagent-driven-development | executing-plans
  → both require using-git-worktrees first (isolated workspace)
  → per task: TDD (subagents told to follow it), requesting-code-review templates
  → both terminate by invoking finishing-a-development-branch
finishing-a-development-branch
  → merge locally | push + PR | keep | discard (+ worktree cleanup)
```

**Cross-cutting:** `verification-before-completion` fires before any "done/fixed/passing" claim; `systematic-debugging` fires on any bug before fixes (links into TDD Phase 4); `receiving-code-review` mediates feedback; `using-superpowers` is the SessionStart router that makes skill invocation compulsory (including a graph node forcing brainstorming before EnterPlanMode). `using-superpowers` also encodes priority: process skills (brainstorming, debugging) before implementation skills.

**Notable mechanism:** the lifecycle handoff lives in artifacts, not just skills — the plan document header tells *future agents in fresh sessions* which skill to use. Checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax in plans serves as cross-session progress tracking.

## 3. Sub-agent usage

Three distinct patterns:

**A. One-subagent-per-task with two-stage review loop** (`subagent-driven-development`):
- Controller reads the plan once, extracts ALL tasks with full text upfront; subagents are *never* told to read the plan file ("Make subagent read plan file" is a listed red flag).
- Per task: dispatch implementer (general-purpose Task tool, `implementer-prompt.md`) → implementer can ask questions *before and during* work → implements + tests + commits + self-reviews → dispatch **spec compliance reviewer** → then (only after spec ✅) **code quality reviewer** → reviewer-found issues go back to the *same* implementer, then re-review. Strict ordering: quality review before spec compliance passes is a named red flag.
- Implementer status protocol: `DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT`, with controller playbook per status (BLOCKED → more context / more capable model / split task / escalate to human).
- **Model routing built in:** mechanical 1–2-file tasks → cheap model; integration → standard; architecture/review → most capable.
- Spec reviewer prompt contains a deliberate distrust framing: "The implementer finished suspiciously quickly. Their report may be incomplete... DO NOT take their word." Verify by reading code, not the report.
- Never dispatch multiple *implementation* subagents in parallel (conflict risk); continuous execution with no "should I continue?" check-ins.
- After all tasks: one final whole-implementation reviewer, then finishing-a-development-branch.

**B. Parallel investigation agents** (`dispatching-parallel-agents`): one agent per independent problem domain (e.g. 3 unrelated failing test files), dispatched concurrently; prompts must be focused, self-contained, constrained ("Do NOT change production code"), with specified return format; controller verifies no conflicts + runs full suite after.

**C. Reviewer-as-subagent** (`requesting-code-review`): dispatch a "Senior Code Reviewer" persona with `{DESCRIPTION, PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS, BASE_SHA, HEAD_SHA}`; reviews the git diff range, returns Strengths / Issues (Critical/Important/Minor) / Recommendations / "Ready to merge? Yes|No|With fixes".

**Shared philosophy (stated identically in both subagent skills):** subagents never inherit session context/history — the controller hand-crafts exactly the context they need; this both keeps them focused and preserves the controller's context for coordination. Worktree isolation is a *prerequisite of the workflow* (via using-git-worktrees), not per-subagent — subagents share the one worktree, serialized.

## 4. Authoring style

- **Frontmatter: just two fields** — `name` and `description`. No version, author, length targets, or taxonomy. Descriptions are trigger-condition-shaped, third person: "Use when X, before Y - does Z" (some add intensity: brainstorming's starts "You MUST use this before any creative work").
- **Length:** 70–371 lines for workflow skills (median ~190); writing-skills is the outlier at 655. The pack's own guidance (writing-skills): keep sections <150 lines, SKILL.md <200 lines preferred, push details to companion files in the skill dir loaded on demand (progressive disclosure).
- **Recurring structural devices:**
  - **"Iron Law" blocks** — single-sentence absolutes in code fences (TDD, verification, debugging) plus "Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule."
  - **Graphviz `dot` digraphs** as machine-readable flowcharts for decision logic and process loops (brainstorming, subagent-driven, using-superpowers, dispatching-parallel, TDD). There's a whole `graphviz-conventions.dot` style guide.
  - **Rationalization tables** (Excuse | Reality two-column) — explicitly designed to pre-empt the agent's own excuses ("I'm confident" → "Confidence ≠ evidence"; "Emergency, no time" → "Systematic is FASTER").
  - **Red Flags sections** — "Never:" / "Always:" bullet lists, or thought-pattern tables ("if you catch yourself thinking X, STOP").
  - **Quick Reference tables** (situation → action).
  - **Common Mistakes** with Problem/Fix pairs.
  - **Announce-at-start lines**: "I'm using the X skill to Y" — makes skill use observable to the human.
  - **Checklists mapped to TodoWrite** (brainstorming mandates a todo per checklist item; using-superpowers's flowchart enforces this generally).
  - ✅/❌ contrastive example pairs for behavioral patterns.
  - Concrete worked example transcripts (subagent-driven has a full 70-line simulated session).
  - "Real-World Impact" sections citing session data ("first-time fix rate 95% vs 40%", "from 24 failure memories").
- **Tone:** imperative, absolutist, anti-rationalization; moralized stakes ("Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency"; "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced"). Persuasion is deliberate — `writing-skills/persuasion-principles.md` documents the influence techniques used. Addresses the user as "your human partner" throughout.
- **What makes them effective/terse:** every section is either a gate, a table, a flowchart, or a prompt template — almost no expository filler; exact bash commands with expected output; deterministic decision tables (e.g. finishing-a-development-branch's environment-detection table keyed on `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`); skills are *tested* — writing-skills mandates TDD-for-docs with subagent pressure-testing (`testing-skills-with-subagents.md`, `test-pressure-*.md` fixtures) before deployment.
- **Distribution trick:** the SessionStart hook injects the entire `using-superpowers` skill into context wrapped in `<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>`, making the dispatcher always-loaded while everything else stays lazy.

## 5. Delivery/execution capabilities in detail

**executing-plans (inline mode, 70 lines — deliberately thin):** load plan → critical review (raise concerns before starting) → TodoWrite per task → follow steps *exactly* → run specified verifications → finishing-a-development-branch. Stop conditions: blocker, critical plan gap, unclear instruction, repeated verification failure — "ask rather than guess." The skill itself says: if subagents are available, use subagent-driven-development instead. Never start on main/master without explicit consent.

**subagent-driven-development:** see §3A. Key delivery properties: continuous autonomous execution (the README claims multi-hour autonomous runs), per-task commit discipline (implementer commits within the task), review loops that must re-run until ✅, controller never fixes code manually ("context pollution" — dispatch a fix subagent instead).

**Verification model — three reinforcing layers:**
1. *Plan-level:* every plan step embeds its own verification command + expected output ("Run: pytest ... Expected: FAIL with 'function not defined'"); TDD red-green is baked into the step template.
2. *Task-level:* implementer self-review checklist (completeness/quality/discipline/testing) + two independent reviewer subagents reading actual code/diffs, not reports.
3. *Claim-level:* verification-before-completion's gate function (IDENTIFY command → RUN fresh → READ full output → VERIFY → only then claim) applies to any success claim, including "Agent completed" (requires checking VCS diff, never trusting the agent's report) and regression tests (require demonstrated red-green: pass → revert fix → must fail → restore → pass).

**Git/branches/PRs:**
- Isolation first: using-git-worktrees runs before execution. Detection order: already-isolated check (`GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, with submodule guard) → native harness tool (EnterWorktree etc. — "the #1 mistake" is using raw git when a native tool exists) → manual `git worktree add` under `.worktrees/` (must verify gitignored, commit .gitignore change) → sandbox fallback to in-place. Then auto setup (npm/cargo/pip/go) + clean baseline test run before any work.
- Commits: frequent, per plan step ("Step 5: Commit" with exact `git add`/`git commit` commands in the plan).
- Finishing: tests must pass before options are even presented; exactly 4 options (3 on detached HEAD — no local merge). PR path: `git push -u origin` + `gh pr create` with Summary + Test Plan body; worktree preserved for PR iteration. Merge path: merge → re-run tests on merged result → only then remove worktree → delete branch (ordering prevents `branch -d` failure). Discard requires the user to type the literal word "discard". Cleanup respects provenance: only remove worktrees superpowers created (`.worktrees/`, `worktrees/`, `~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/`); harness-owned workspaces are left alone. Never force-push without explicit request.

## 6. Gaps — what it does NOT cover

- **No product/portfolio layer:** nothing upstream of "an idea arrives" — no idea triage/scoring, prioritization, roadmapping, capacity planning, OKR/initiative shaping, or appetite/kill conditions. Brainstorming assumes the decision to build is already made.

# obra/superpowers — Structured Analysis

**Source analyzed:** `/Users/anton/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/5.1.0/` (installed plugin, version 5.1.0). Skills at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, hooks at `hooks/`, marketplace = `superpowers-marketplace`.

---

## 1. Skill inventory (14 skills)

| Skill | Lines | One-line purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `brainstorming` | 164 | Turn an idea into an approved design/spec via one-question-at-a-time dialogue; HARD-GATE: no implementation until user approves design. |
| `writing-plans` | 152 | Convert approved spec into a plan of bite-sized (2–5 min) TDD steps with exact paths, full code, no placeholders. |
| `executing-plans` | 70 | Inline (no-subagent) plan execution: load plan, review critically, execute tasks, stop on blockers. Explicitly second-choice to subagent-driven. |
| `subagent-driven-development` | 279 | Execute a plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task + two-stage review (spec compliance, then code quality) per task. |
| `dispatching-parallel-agents` | 182 | One agent per independent problem domain, dispatched concurrently (e.g. 3 unrelated failing test files). |
| `test-driven-development` | 371 | Strict red-green-refactor; Iron Law: "NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST" — code written before test must be deleted. |
| `systematic-debugging` | 296 | Four phases (root cause → pattern analysis → hypothesis → implementation); 3+ failed fixes = question the architecture. |
| `using-git-worktrees` | 215 | Ensure isolated workspace: detect existing isolation → prefer native tools (EnterWorktree) → fall back to `git worktree add` under `.worktrees/`. |
| `finishing-a-development-branch` | 251 | End-of-work ritual: verify tests → detect environment → present exactly 4 options (merge local / push+PR / keep / discard) → cleanup. |
| `requesting-code-review` | 103 | Dispatch a code-reviewer subagent with git SHA range + template; mandatory after each task and before merge. |
| `receiving-code-review` | 213 | Verify-before-implement feedback handling; forbids performative agreement ("You're absolutely right!"); skeptical of external reviewers. |
| `verification-before-completion` | 139 | Iron Law: "NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE" — run the command in this message or don't claim it. |
| `using-superpowers` | 117 | Meta-skill injected at SessionStart; "even 1% chance a skill applies → MUST invoke"; rationalization table; process skills before implementation skills. |
| `writing-skills` | 655 | How to author/test skills: TDD-for-docs, CSO (Claude Search Optimization), token budgets (<150 lines/section), bulletproofing against rationalization, pressure-testing with subagents. |

**Supporting files (not SKILL.md):**
- `subagent-driven-development/`: `implementer-prompt.md`, `spec-reviewer-prompt.md`, `code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md`
- `requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md` (4.7K reviewer prompt template)
- `systematic-debugging/`: `root-cause-tracing.md`, `defense-in-depth.md`, `condition-based-waiting.md` (+example.ts), `find-polluter.sh`, pressure-test fixtures (`test-pressure-1..3.md`)
- `test-driven-development/testing-anti-patterns.md` (8.1K)
- `writing-skills/`: `anthropic-best-practices.md` (44.7K), `graphviz-conventions.dot`, `persuasion-principles.md`, `testing-skills-with-subagents.md` (12.3K)
- `brainstorming/visual-companion.md` (browser-based mockup companion)
- Hooks: `hooks/hooks.json` (SessionStart on startup|clear|compact) + `hooks/session-start` (bash script that injects the full text of `using-superpowers` SKILL.md as additionalContext — multi-platform: Claude Code/Cursor/Copilot detection)
- Multi-harness packaging: `.claude-plugin/`, `.codex-plugin/`, `.cursor-plugin/`, `.opencode/`, `GEMINI.md`

## 2. Lifecycle coverage and chaining

**Covered stages:** idea → design/spec → plan → execute → per-task review → finish (merge/PR). Plus orthogonal disciplines: TDD, debugging, verification, review reception.

**The canonical chain (each skill explicitly names the next as "REQUIRED SUB-SKILL"):**

```
brainstorming
  → writes spec to docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md
  → user-approval gate → invokes writing-plans (the ONLY allowed next skill)
writing-plans
  → writes plan to docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature>.md
  → plan header itself embeds: "REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: use subagent-driven-development
    (recommended) or executing-plans"
  → offers user choice: Subagent-Driven vs Inline
subagent-driven-development | executing-plans
  → both require using-git-worktrees first (isolated workspace)
  → per task: TDD (subagents told to follow it), requesting-code-review templates
  → both terminate by invoking finishing-a-development-branch
finishing-a-development-branch
  → merge locally | push + PR | keep | discard (+ worktree cleanup)
```

**Cross-cutting:** `verification-before-completion` fires before any "done/fixed/passing" claim; `systematic-debugging` fires on any bug before fixes (links into TDD Phase 4); `receiving-code-review` mediates feedback; `using-superpowers` is the SessionStart router that makes skill invocation compulsory (including a graph node forcing brainstorming before EnterPlanMode). `using-superpowers` also encodes priority: process skills (brainstorming, debugging) before implementation skills.

**Notable mechanism:** the lifecycle handoff lives in artifacts, not just skills — the plan document header tells *future agents in fresh sessions* which skill to use. Checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax in plans serves as cross-session progress tracking.

## 3. Sub-agent usage

Three distinct patterns:

**A. One-subagent-per-task with two-stage review loop** (`subagent-driven-development`):
- Controller reads the plan once, extracts ALL tasks with full text upfront; subagents are *never* told to read the plan file ("Make subagent read plan file" is a listed red flag).
- Per task: dispatch implementer (general-purpose Task tool, `implementer-prompt.md`) → implementer can ask questions *before and during* work → implements + tests + commits + self-reviews → dispatch **spec compliance reviewer** → then (only after spec ✅) **code quality reviewer** → reviewer-found issues go back to the *same* implementer, then re-review. Strict ordering: quality review before spec compliance passes is a named red flag.
- Implementer status protocol: `DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT`, with controller playbook per status (BLOCKED → more context / more capable model / split task / escalate to human).
- **Model routing built in:** mechanical 1–2-file tasks → cheap model; integration → standard; architecture/review → most capable.
- Spec reviewer prompt contains a deliberate distrust framing: "The implementer finished suspiciously quickly. Their report may be incomplete... DO NOT take their word." Verify by reading code, not the report.
- Never dispatch multiple *implementation* subagents in parallel (conflict risk); continuous execution with no "should I continue?" check-ins.
- After all tasks: one final whole-implementation reviewer, then finishing-a-development-branch.

**B. Parallel investigation agents** (`dispatching-parallel-agents`): one agent per independent problem domain (e.g. 3 unrelated failing test files), dispatched concurrently; prompts must be focused, self-contained, constrained ("Do NOT change production code"), with specified return format; controller verifies no conflicts + runs full suite after.

**C. Reviewer-as-subagent** (`requesting-code-review`): dispatch a "Senior Code Reviewer" persona with `{DESCRIPTION, PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS, BASE_SHA, HEAD_SHA}`; reviews the git diff range, returns Strengths / Issues (Critical/Important/Minor) / Recommendations / "Ready to merge? Yes|No|With fixes".

**Shared philosophy (stated identically in both subagent skills):** subagents never inherit session context/history — the controller hand-crafts exactly the context they need; this both keeps them focused and preserves the controller's context for coordination. Worktree isolation is a *prerequisite of the workflow* (via using-git-worktrees), not per-subagent — subagents share the one worktree, serialized.

## 4. Authoring style

- **Frontmatter: just two fields** — `name` and `description`. No version, author, length targets, or taxonomy. Descriptions are trigger-condition-shaped, third person: "Use when X, before Y - does Z" (some add intensity: brainstorming's starts "You MUST use this before any creative work").
- **Length:** 70–371 lines for workflow skills (median ~190); writing-skills is the outlier at 655. The pack's own guidance (writing-skills): keep sections <150 lines, SKILL.md <200 lines preferred, push details to companion files in the skill dir loaded on demand (progressive disclosure).
- **Recurring structural devices:**
  - **"Iron Law" blocks** — single-sentence absolutes in code fences (TDD, verification, debugging) plus "Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule."
  - **Graphviz `dot` digraphs** as machine-readable flowcharts for decision logic and process loops (brainstorming, subagent-driven, using-superpowers, dispatching-parallel, TDD). There's a whole `graphviz-conventions.dot` style guide.
  - **Rationalization tables** (Excuse | Reality two-column) — explicitly designed to pre-empt the agent's own excuses ("I'm confident" → "Confidence ≠ evidence"; "Emergency, no time" → "Systematic is FASTER").
  - **Red Flags sections** — "Never:" / "Always:" bullet lists, or thought-pattern tables ("if you catch yourself thinking X, STOP").
  - **Quick Reference tables** (situation → action).
  - **Common Mistakes** with Problem/Fix pairs.
  - **Announce-at-start lines**: "I'm using the X skill to Y" — makes skill use observable to the human.
  - **Checklists mapped to TodoWrite** (brainstorming mandates a todo per checklist item; using-superpowers's flowchart enforces this generally).
  - ✅/❌ contrastive example pairs for behavioral patterns.
  - Concrete worked example transcripts (subagent-driven has a full 70-line simulated session).
  - "Real-World Impact" sections citing session data ("first-time fix rate 95% vs 40%", "from 24 failure memories").
- **Tone:** imperative, absolutist, anti-rationalization; moralized stakes ("Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency"; "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced"). Persuasion is deliberate — `writing-skills/persuasion-principles.md` documents the influence techniques used. Addresses the user as "your human partner" throughout.
- **What makes them effective/terse:** every section is either a gate, a table, a flowchart, or a prompt template — almost no expository filler; exact bash commands with expected output; deterministic decision tables (e.g. finishing-a-development-branch's environment-detection table keyed on `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`); skills are *tested* — writing-skills mandates TDD-for-docs with subagent pressure-testing (`testing-skills-with-subagents.md`, `test-pressure-*.md` fixtures) before deployment.
- **Distribution trick:** the SessionStart hook injects the entire `using-superpowers` skill into context wrapped in `<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>`, making the dispatcher always-loaded while everything else stays lazy.

## 5. Delivery/execution capabilities in detail

**executing-plans (inline mode, 70 lines — deliberately thin):** load plan → critical review (raise concerns before starting) → TodoWrite per task → follow steps *exactly* → run specified verifications → finishing-a-development-branch. Stop conditions: blocker, critical plan gap, unclear instruction, repeated verification failure — "ask rather than guess." The skill itself says: if subagents are available, use subagent-driven-development instead. Never start on main/master without explicit consent.

**subagent-driven-development:** see §3A. Key delivery properties: continuous autonomous execution (the README claims multi-hour autonomous runs), per-task commit discipline (implementer commits within the task), review loops that must re-run until ✅, controller never fixes code manually ("context pollution" — dispatch a fix subagent instead).

**Verification model — three reinforcing layers:**
1. *Plan-level:* every plan step embeds its own verification command + expected output ("Run: pytest ... Expected: FAIL with 'function not defined'"); TDD red-green is baked into the step template.
2. *Task-level:* implementer self-review checklist (completeness/quality/discipline/testing) + two independent reviewer subagents reading actual code/diffs, not reports.
3. *Claim-level:* verification-before-completion's gate function (IDENTIFY command → RUN fresh → READ full output → VERIFY → only then claim) applies to any success claim, including "Agent completed" (requires checking VCS diff, never trusting the agent's report) and regression tests (require demonstrated red-green: pass → revert fix → must fail → restore → pass).

**Git/branches/PRs:**
- Isolation first: using-git-worktrees runs before execution. Detection order: already-isolated check (`GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, with submodule guard) → native harness tool (EnterWorktree etc. — "the #1 mistake" is using raw git when a native tool exists) → manual `git worktree add` under `.worktrees/` (must verify gitignored, commit .gitignore change) → sandbox fallback to in-place. Then auto setup (npm/cargo/pip/go) + clean baseline test run before any work.
- Commits: frequent, per plan step ("Step 5: Commit" with exact `git add`/`git commit` commands in the plan).
- Finishing: tests must pass before options are even presented; exactly 4 options (3 on detached HEAD — no local merge). PR path: `git push -u origin` + `gh pr create` with Summary + Test Plan body; worktree preserved for PR iteration. Merge path: merge → re-run tests on merged result → only then remove worktree → delete branch (ordering prevents `branch -d` failure). Discard requires the user to type the literal word "discard". Cleanup respects provenance: only remove worktrees superpowers created (`.worktrees/`, `worktrees/`, `~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/`); harness-owned workspaces are left alone. Never force-push without explicit request.

## 6. Gaps — what it does NOT cover

- **No product/portfolio layer:** nothing upstream of "an idea arrives" — no idea triage/scoring, prioritization, roadmapping, capacity planning, OKR/initiative shaping, or appetite/kill conditions. Brainstorming assumes the decision to build is already made.
- **No issue-tracker integration:** no Linear/Jira/GitHub-Issues lifecycle, no cycle/backlog governance. State lives entirely in markdown plan files + checkboxes + git.
- **No multi-PR / stacked-delivery model:** one branch, one plan, one finish. No PR stacking, no auto-merge policy, no PR-body conventions beyond a minimal template, no release/versioning/changelog/deploy skills.
- **No CI/CD, ops, or post-ship coverage:** no pipeline authoring, monitoring/observability, incident response, rollback, feature flags, or post-launch evidence loops.
- **No estimation/sizing/scheduling:** tasks are "bite-sized" by fiat; no sizing rubric, no dependency-graph or critical-path planning, no parallel execution of *implementation* tasks (explicitly forbidden — execution is strictly serial; parallelism is reserved for independent investigations).
- **No security/performance/accessibility specialist reviews:** the code-reviewer template mentions security/scalability as bullet points but there are no dedicated skills.
- **No frontend/design, data, or domain-specific engineering skills** in this plugin (README references frontend-design/mcp-builder as things brainstorming must NOT invoke — they live elsewhere).
- **No documentation/ADR skill** beyond the spec and plan artifacts; no human-facing rendering of artifacts.
- **Thin requirements rigor:** specs have a self-review (placeholders/consistency/ambiguity) but no acceptance-criteria formalism, no measurable success criteria, no adversarial plan review by an independent agent (plan review is a self-checklist; note `writing-plans/plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md` and `brainstorming/spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md` exist as templates but the SKILL.md flow uses inline self-review).
- **Minimal frontmatter/metadata:** no versioning, provenance, principle citations, or length governance fields per skill — conventions are enforced by prose in writing-skills, not by schema.

## RAW FINDINGS FOR SYNTHESIS

1. **Coverage is front-heavy**: All 14 skills plus sub-agent sit in Define/Plan/Decide/Review/Verify/Ship phases (idea → spec → plan → PR prep). Zero coverage of build, deploy, or post-launch. **Intentional scoping per README; intended pairing with `addyosmani/agent-skills`.**

2. **Three skills exceed 300-line target** (plan-review 369, initiative-shape 310, roadmap-shape 303). All three are load-bearing and compress efficiently; no redundancy found. No splits recommended.

3. **Tracker-agnosticism is enforced at architecture level**: initiative-shape (the heaviest skill) checks at runtime whether a tracker binding is present; emits markdown or hands off to Workflow pack. **Zero coupling to Linear or other specific tracker in skill code.**

4. **Single agent file** (code-reviewer, 131 lines) provides pre-commit multi-axis review. No skill dispatches agents; agents are loaded by Workflow pack governance. **Agent design is sound: posture defined, context pre-loaded before seeing diff, model tier justified (Frontier = orchestrator).**

5. **Hooks are deterministic and mechanical** (2 total; 165 lines): PR signal-suppression detection, commit-time task annotation counting. No false positives by design.

6. **Execution capabilities are minimal by scope**: pr-prepare (context writing), verify-implementation (AC gate), code-reviewer (review before merge). No build/debug/deploy coverage. **This is intentional; README explicitly frames Shaper as Define/Plan/Design/Review, delegating Build/Ship/Deploy to execution pack.**

7. **Principle embedding is heavy**: Most skills embed 6–10+ principles as red flags, rationalisation rebuttals, gates. Only 3 standalone artefacts exist (PRODUCT_RULES, eng-principles-universal, eng-principles-agentic). **Follows authoring-learnings.md heuristic: a principle earns standalone artefact only when it has workflow + verifiable failure mode + agent reason to miss it.**

8. **References are well-organized and cited**: 10 reference files total (1,196 lines). No duplication of reference material within skills.

9. **SessionStart hook is elegant**: Loads meta-skill on every session; agent learns task routing from skill discovery flowchart. No push of all rules at session start.

10. **Frontmatter discipline is strict**: All 14 skills + 1 agent + 2 hooks have complete frontmatter with predecessor/relation declarations. Traceability is durable.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/anton/.claude/plugins/cache/addy-agent-skills/agent-skills/2e0dfbfb436e/skills/interview-me

# Interview Me

## Overview

What people ask for and what they actually want are different things. They ask for "a dashboard" because that's what one asks for, not because a dashboard solves their problem. They say "make it faster" without a number to hit.

The cheapest moment to find this gap is before any plan, spec, or code exists. Once you've started building, switching costs are real, and the user will rationalize the wrong thing into a "good enough" thing. The misfit gets locked in.

This skill closes the gap before it costs anything. The other Define-phase skills assume you already know roughly what you want: `idea-refine` generates variations from an idea, `spec-driven-development` writes the requirements down, `doubt-driven-development` stress-tests a plan after you've drafted one. Interview-me is the part before all of those, where you ask one question at a time, with your best guess attached, until you can predict what the user is going to say before they say it.

## When to Use

Apply this skill when:

- The ask is missing at least one of: **who** the user is, **why** they want it, what **success** looks like, what the binding **constraint** is
- The request is conventional rather than specific ("build me X", "make it faster") and you can't unpack the convention without guessing
- You're tempted to start with assumptions you haven't surfaced
- The user hasn't said which value they're optimizing for when two reasonable ones are in tension (simplicity vs. flexibility, cost vs. speed)
- The user explicitly invokes: "interview me", "grill me", "before we start, are we sure?", "stress-test my thinking"

**When NOT to use:**

- The ask is unambiguous and self-contained ("rename this variable", "fix this typo")
- The user has explicitly asked for speed over verification
- Pure information requests ("how does X work?", "what does this code do?")
- Mechanical operations (renames, formats, file moves)
- You already have ≥95% confidence; re-read the stop condition below before assuming you don't

## Loading Constraints

This skill needs a live, responsive user. **Do not invoke in non-interactive contexts** like CI pipelines, scheduled runs, `/loop`, or autonomous-loop. If you're in one of those and the ask is underspecified, flag that as a blocker for the user instead of guessing.

## The Process

### Step 1: Hypothesize, with a confidence number

Before asking anything, write down your current best read of what the user wants in **one sentence**, plus an honest confidence number (0–100%):

```
HYPOTHESIS: You want a way to answer "how are we doing?" in standup, and "dashboard" was the convention that came to mind.
CONFIDENCE: ~30% — missing: who it's for, what "metrics" means in context, and what success looks like
```

The number forces honesty. If you wrote down a high number but can't actually predict the user's reactions to the next three questions you'd ask, the number is wrong. Start at the confidence level you can defend.

When confidence is below ~70%, append a brief reason on the same line — what's still unresolved or missing. This tells the user exactly what the interview needs to surface, and prevents the number from being a vague signal.

### Step 2: Ask one question at a time, each with a guess attached

Format:

```
Q: <one focused question>
GUESS: <your hypothesis for the answer, with the reasoning that produced it>
```

Wait for the user to react before asking the next question.

**Why one at a time, not a batch:**

- The user can't react to your hypotheses if you bury them in a list
- Batches encourage skim-reading and surface answers
- The third question often depends on the answer to the first; asking them all at once locks in the wrong framing
- The user's energy for thinking carefully is finite; spend it one question at a time

**Why attach a guess:**

- The user reacts faster to a wrong guess than they generate an answer from scratch
- It commits you to a hypothesis you can be visibly wrong about, which keeps you honest
- It surfaces *your* assumptions, which is what the interview is meant to expose

The risk here is a polite user agreeing with your guess to be agreeable. Mitigate by being visibly willing to be wrong, and occasionally guess in a direction you expect the user to push back on.

### Step 3: Listen for "want vs. should want"

The most dangerous answers are the ones where the user says what a thoughtful answer *sounds like* rather than what they actually want. Watch for:

- Answers that pattern-match best-practice talk ("I want it to be scalable", "clean architecture") without specifics
- Answers that defer to convention ("the way most apps do it", "the standard approach")
- Phrases like "I should probably…", "I think I'm supposed to…", "good engineering practice says…"
- Buzzwords as goals — when "modern", "scalable", "robust" are the answer instead of a specific outcome

When you hear these, the question to ask is:

> *"If you didn't have to justify this to anyone, what would you actually want?"*

That single question often does more work than the previous five.

### Step 4: Restate intent in the user's own words

When your confidence is high, write back what you now think the user wants. Keep it tight (5–8 lines), use their language where possible, and structure it so the user can confirm or correct line by line:

```
Here's what I now think you want:

- Outcome:      <one line>
- User:         <one line — who benefits>
- Why now:      <one line — what changed>
- Success:      <one line — how we know it worked>
- Constraint:   <one line — the binding limit>
- Out of scope: <one line — what we're explicitly not doing>

Yes / no / refine?
```

Including "Out of scope" is non-negotiable. Half of misalignment is silent disagreement about what is *not* being built.

### Step 5: Confirm — explicit yes, not "whatever you think"

The gate is an explicit "yes." The following are **not** yes:

- "Whatever you think is best." → The user is delegating, which means they don't have 95% confidence either. Re-ask with two concrete options framed as a choice.
- "Sounds good." → Ambiguous. Ask: "Anything you'd refine?" Silence isn't confirmation.
- "Sure, let's go." → Often a polite exit, not an endorsement. Same follow-up.
- Silence followed by "okay let's start." → The user has given up on the interview, not converged. Stop and ask whether you've missed something.

If they correct you, fold the correction in and restate. Loop until you get an explicit yes.

### The 95% Confidence Stop

You're done when you can answer yes to this:

> *Can I predict the user's reaction to the next three questions I would ask?*

If yes, you have shared understanding. Stop interviewing and produce the restate. If no, you're not done; ask the next question.

This is a checkable test, not a vibe. It also has a floor: if you've gone several rounds and still can't predict, that's information about the ask, not a reason to keep grinding. Stop and tell the user: "I've asked X questions and I still can't predict your reactions. Something foundational is missing. Want to step back?"

## Output

The output of this skill is a **confirmed statement of intent**: the restate from Step 4, with an explicit yes from Step 5. That's the deliverable. Specs, plans, and task lists are downstream; they consume the intent this skill produces.

If the user wants the intent to persist (a multi-session project, a handoff to another collaborator), offer to save it to `docs/intent/[topic].md`. Only save if they confirm.

## Example

A short before-and-after.

**Without `interview-me`:**

```
User:  build me a dashboard for our metrics
Agent: <starts proposing chart libraries and layouts>
```

The agent has assumed: who it's for, what metrics, what "for our team" means, what success looks like. None of these are stated. Every assumption is a place the user can later say "that's not what I meant."

**With `interview-me`:**

```
User: build me a dashboard for our metrics

Agent:
HYPOTHESIS: You want a way to answer "how are we doing?" in standup, and "dashboard" came to mind because that's the conventional answer.
CONFIDENCE: ~30% — missing: who it's for, what "metrics" are, and what success looks like

Q:     When you say "how are we doing?", who's asking — you alone, the engineering team in standup, or up the chain (e.g., your manager, an exec, a board)?
GUESS: engineering team in standup, because "we" usually scopes that way and standups are where this question gets asked. If it's for execs the metrics and the framing change a lot.

User: It's actually for me. I keep losing track of which experiments are running and what their early signal looks like.

Agent:
Updated read: not a team dashboard at all. It's a personal experiment tracker. Confidence: ~60% — still missing: what "early signal" means and what done looks like.

Q:     Is the gap that you don't know which experiments exist, or that you can't see their results in one place?
GUESS: the second one. You have a list of experiments somewhere, but their results live in five different tools, and reconciling them by hand is what you're tired of.

User: First one actually. I literally don't have a list. They're spread across different docs.

Agent: <continues>
```

Two questions in, the agent has discovered the actual ask isn't "a dashboard." It's "a list." Different artifact, different scope, different work. The dashboard would have been wrong.

## Interaction with Other Skills

- **`idea-refine`**: downstream. If the confirmed intent is "I want X but I don't know how to scope it," hand off to `idea-refine` to generate variations against the now-explicit intent.
- **`spec-driven-development`**: downstream. If the confirmed intent is concrete ("I want X for Y users with Z success criteria"), hand off to `spec-driven-development` to write it down.
- **`planning-and-task-breakdown`**: two hops downstream of this skill (after the spec).
- **`doubt-driven-development`**: opposite end of the timeline. Interview-me is pre-decision intent extraction; doubt-driven is post-decision artifact review. Both catch divergence, but at different moments.
- **`source-driven-development`**: orthogonal. Interview-me clarifies what the user wants; SDD verifies framework facts. They don't compete.

## Common Rationalizations

| Rationalization | Reality |
|---|---|
| "The ask is clear enough" | If you can't write the user's desired outcome in one sentence right now, the ask isn't clear. Run Step 1 before deciding. |
| "Asking too many questions wastes their time" | Time wasted by 4–6 targeted questions is small. Time wasted by building the wrong thing is enormous, and the user is the one bearing that cost. |
| "I'll figure it out as I build" | Switching costs after code exists are 10x what they are now. Discovery during implementation is rework. |
| "They said 'whatever you think,' so I should just decide" | "Whatever you think" is delegation, not decision. Re-ask with two concrete options as a choice. |
| "I should give them several options to pick from" | Options work when the user knows what they want and is choosing between trade-offs. They don't know what they want yet. Listing options widens the search; asking narrows it. |
| "If I attach my guess, I'm leading them" | Leading is the point. Reacting is faster than generating from scratch. The risk is sycophancy, not leading; mitigate by being visibly willing to be wrong. |
| "We've talked enough, I get it" | Test it: can you predict their reaction to the next three questions? If not, you don't get it yet. |
| "The user said yes, we're done" | If the yes followed a vague restate or an open-ended "sounds good," the yes is hollow. Restate concretely and re-confirm. |

## Red Flags

- Three or more questions in a single message: that's batching, not interviewing
- A question without your hypothesis attached: that's surveying, not committing
- Accepting "whatever you think is best" as a terminal answer
- Producing a spec, plan, or task list before the user has explicitly confirmed your restate
- Questions framed as "what would be best practice?" instead of "what do you actually want?"
- The user gives a sophistication-signaling answer ("scalable", "clean", "modern") and you accept it without probing whether it's what they actually want
- Three or more rounds without your confidence visibly rising: you're asking the wrong questions, step back and reframe
- A confidence number below ~70% with no reason attached: the user can't help close the gap if they don't know what's missing
- Saving the intent doc before the user has confirmed (the doc itself implies a yes the user didn't give)
- Skipping the "Out of scope" line in the restate (silent disagreement about non-goals is half of misalignment)

## Verification

After applying interview-me:

- [ ] An explicit hypothesis with a confidence number was stated in the first turn
- [ ] Every confidence number below ~70% was accompanied by a one-line reason (what's still unresolved or missing)
- [ ] Questions were asked one at a time, each with the agent's guess attached
- [ ] At least one "what would you actually want if you didn't have to justify it?" probe ran when the user gave a sophistication-signaling or convention-signaling answer
- [ ] A concrete restate (Outcome / User / Why now / Success / Constraint / Out of scope) was written back to the user
- [ ] The user confirmed the restate with an explicit yes (not "whatever you think," not "sounds good," not silence)
- [ ] At the stop point, the agent could predict reactions to the next three questions it would ask
- [ ] Any handoff to a downstream skill (`idea-refine`, `spec-driven-development`) was framed in terms of the confirmed intent, not the original underspecified ask

content.text:
Yes — I think drain-cycle should be re-scoped, and the cross-model point is exactly why. Here's my read:

**The split that makes sense: drain-cycle owns *processes*, Shaper owns *workflow*.**

Claude Code sub-agents (the Agent tool) can only ever spawn Claude models. drain-cycle spawns whole CLI processes — today `claude -p`, tomorrow `codex exec` or a kimi/deepseek wrapper. Those are different layers, and right now drain-cycle blurs them: its prompt template hardcodes the intra-issue workflow ("run /code-review-and-quality, fix findings, commit, push, mark Done"). That workflow prose is exactly what should live in skills instead.

Re-scoped, drain-cycle keeps only what a process-level supervisor can uniquely do: cycle selection and topological ordering, worktree setup, **vendor-agnostic worker spawning**, token/time/cost guardrails with SIGKILL, halt/resume, run logs and grading. Its prompt shrinks to roughly "you are working issue X in worktree Y; follow `/ship:work`" — one skill reference instead of an inlined procedure. That makes the workflow versionable in the pack, testable interactively, and identical whether you or a worker runs it.

**The sub-agent wrinkle your question exposes:** if a skill says "dispatch the security-auditor sub-agent," that step only executes on Claude Code. A codex or kimi worker can't run it. The fix is how superpowers structures it — personas live as standalone prompt files (`agents/security-auditor.md` is a role prompt + output contract, not Claude-specific machinery), and the skill defines the *step* ("get an adversarial security review of the diff; output format Z") with two bindings: Agent-tool dispatch when available, inline-sequential self-review with the same persona prompt when not. Same artefact, degraded gracefully.

**And the cross-model delegation gets *more* interesting, not less:** once drain-cycle is a vendor-agnostic spawner, it can spawn *reviewer* processes too — Claude implements, codex adversarially reviews, or vice versa. Genuinely-different-model review is a stronger correctness signal than same-model-different-prompt review, which is directly your stated purpose. Sub-agents in skills give you cheap same-session fan-out; drain-cycle gives you expensive cross-vendor adversarial passes for hard tickets. Both, different tiers.

So my answer to the question you paused: **both** — reviewer personas as portable prompt files that skills bind to sub-agents when on Claude Code, *and* drain-cycle re-scoped thinner so cross-model workers can follow the same skills.
